analysis.evidence: The opening כִּי introduces the serpent’s reason for his preceding denial: “for God knows.” The second כִּי introduces what God knows.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected conjunction with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In יֹדֵעַ אֱלֹהִים, God is the subject. The following כִּי introduces what the serpent says God knows, namely that when the addressees eat from the tree, their eyes will be opened and they will be like God, knowing good and evil.
analysis.morphology: Qal active participle, masculine singular absolute, used predicatively
analysis.sense: to know that something is the case

analysis.evidence: In יֹדֵעַ אֱלֹהִים, “God knows,” the masculine singular participle יֹדֵעַ agrees with its subject אֱלֹהִים, identifying God as the one who knows.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural absolute noun with singular agreement. It has no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: The marked כִּי follows יֹדֵעַ אֱלֹהִים (“God knows”) and introduces what God knows. The phrase בְּיוֹם אֲכָלְכֶם מִמֶּנּוּ (“when you eat from it”) gives the time within that clause.
analysis.morphology: Subordinating conjunction without a prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: that (what is seen, known or said)

analysis.evidence: בְּיוֹם governs the infinitive construct אֲכָלְכֶם, whose suffix identifies the eaters as “you” (plural). The phrase בְּיוֹם אֲכָלְכֶם מִמֶּנּוּ means “when you eat from it” and specifies when their eyes will open.
analysis.morphology: Noun, masculine singular construct, with prefixed preposition בְּ.
analysis.sense: the time when; on the day that

analysis.evidence: בְּיוֹם אֲכָלְכֶם מִמֶּנּוּ means “when you eat from it.” The suffix identifies the addressees as those who eat, and מִמֶּנּוּ specifies what they eat from.
analysis.morphology: Qal infinitive construct with the second-person masculine plural suffix ־כֶם marking the subject.

draft.change: Add Genesis 3:5 as an example of the existing partitive sense, min-some-of.
draft.definition: With a verb of eating, מִן marks the food of which someone eats a part.
draft.evidence: Genesis 3:5 repeats the suffixed preposition used with the same verb in Genesis 3:3.

analysis.evidence: בְּיוֹם אֲכָלְכֶם מִמֶּנּוּ means “when you eat of it.” The serpent repeats the woman’s לֹא תֹאכְלוּ מִמֶּנּוּ in Genesis 3:3. Her words identify what they would eat as the fruit of the tree.
analysis.morphology: Preposition with a third-person masculine singular pronominal suffix.
analysis.sense: Partitive, marking what someone eats some of.

draft.change: Add the Hebrew verb פָּקַח under פקח with its Niphal sense attested in Genesis 3:5.
draft.definition: In the Niphal, eyes are opened, enabling a person to perceive what was previously unrecognized.
draft.evidence: In Genesis 3:5 the serpent links the opening of the hearers’ eyes with knowing good and evil.

analysis.evidence: עֵינֵיכֶם, “your eyes,” is the subject of וְנִפְקְחוּ. The serpent predicts that their eyes will be opened when they eat, then describes them as יֹדְעֵי טוֹב וָרָע, “knowing good and evil.” This connects the opening of their eyes with a change in what they perceive.
analysis.morphology: וְ prefixed to the Niphal perfect, third person common plural. The ending וּ agrees with עֵינֵיכֶם, “your eyes.” The weqatal expresses the predicted result of eating.
analysis.sense: For eyes to be opened so that a person perceives something previously unrecognized.

analysis.evidence: The serpent promises וְנִפְקְחוּ עֵינֵיכֶם, “your eyes will be opened.” The following phrase יֹדְעֵי טוֹב וָרָע, “knowing good and evil,” explains the opening of their eyes as gaining understanding.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, dual construct, with a second-person masculine plural possessive suffix.

analysis.evidence: The serpent predicts what will follow when the hearers eat. After “your eyes will be opened,” כֵּאלֹהִים describes what they will become like, and יֹדְעֵי טוֹב וָרָע specifies the point of likeness: knowing good and evil.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, second masculine plural, with prefixed conjunction וִ־ (weqatal), expressing a predicted result

analysis.evidence: The serpent opens with יֹדֵעַ אֱלֹהִים, “God knows,” where the participle is singular. Repeating אֱלֹהִים in the comparison favors the same referent. The plural יֹדְעֵי can describe the people addressed by וִהְיִיתֶם, “you will be.” Their knowledge of good and evil is the point of comparison.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition כֵּ־ expresses comparison. The noun is masculine plural absolute in form and refers here to God.

analysis.evidence: The plural participle יֹדְעֵי describes those addressed by וִהְיִיתֶם (“you will be”). Its construct form links it to טוֹב וָרָע (“good and evil”), specifying what they will be able to discern.
analysis.morphology: Qal active participle, masculine plural construct

analysis.evidence: In יֹדְעֵי טוֹב וָרָע, “knowing good and evil,” טוֹב and רָע form a pair of opposites specifying what will be known.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular absolute adjective used substantivally, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: good (and evil): to know, discern or choose

analysis.evidence: In יֹדְעֵי טוֹב וָרָע, “knowing good and evil,” וָ־ joins רָע to טוֹב. Together they name the objects of knowledge, which accounts for the nominal sense.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וָ־ prefixes a masculine singular absolute adjective used substantivally. רָע is the pausal form of רַע.
